# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This follow-up does what good follow-ups should. It registered its analyses before seeing the outcomes, added a stricter hours measure, reports a declining estimate honestly, and directly tests claims made by the two later papers. Its central conclusion, that the per-hour gain shrank but did not disappear, is well supported. The weaker parts are the mediation analysis, which is stated more strongly than the design allows, and a problem in the control group that affects the decay estimate.

## Arithmetic checks

These all reproduce:

| Figure | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden 11, hours | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden 11, per hour | 96.8 / 0.866 = 1.118 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Meetings, treated v control | (7.4 → 3.9) v (7.2 → 7.0) | about 3.3 h net cut, matching month six ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% ✓ |

## Main issues

### 1. The control group was contaminated

At month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their meetings. That makes the control group better from month 15 on, which has two consequences:
- **The 24-month effect is understated.** If the estimate covers months 15–24, those two offices' 4.1% improvement raises the control mean by roughly 1.2 points (2/7 × 4.1). That is a large share of the 2.7-point fall from 12.5% to 9.8%.
- **The mediation estimate is weakened.** Meeting cuts in the control group shrink the meeting contrast.

The decline may therefore be partly the control offices improving, not the treated offices fading. Two reports are needed:
- the main estimates with those two offices excluded, or with their post-audit months excluded;
- their 4.1% gain measured against the other five control offices over the same months, not against their own previous six months.

### 2. The Summary compares two different hours measures

"Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" sets a timesheet figure against a log figure. The like-for-like decline is **12.5% → 9.8%**. The body says this, but the Summary should too.

The decline is also not statistically established. The two confidence intervals (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) overlap heavily. A formal test of the change is needed, with the control contamination taken into account.

### 3. What do the system logs measure?

This determines what the mediation result means.
- **If logs capture only time spent working on cases,** meeting time is already outside the denominator. Cutting meetings could then raise output per log-hour only through fewer interruptions and more focus. That would be a behavioural effect, not an accounting one.
- **But the hours data contradict that reading.** If logs excluded meetings, treated case-work hours should have fallen by much less than total hours: roughly 1 hour out of about 30, given the 3.5-hour meeting cut. Instead, logged hours fell 11%, almost the same as timesheets (12%). That suggests staff stay logged in during meetings, so "active log-in time" includes them.

The definition matters. If meetings are in the denominator, part of the "meetings pathway" is simply arithmetic: unproductive hours were removed. Two further gaps:
- Logs are absent at nine months. The report should say whether baseline log data were retrieved from historical records, as the difference-in-differences requires.
- The nine-month report said meeting data existed only for month six. Here a baseline appears (7.4 and 7.2 hours). Presumably this was reconstructed from calendar history. If so, that resolves my earlier concern about baseline imbalance, but it should be stated.

### 4. The mediation analysis cannot "confirm"

- **It is not independent of the original finding.** The registered test uses the same seven treated offices that produced the exploratory r = 0.71, and it was registered after those results were known. Registering in advance prevents changing the model after seeing outcomes. It does not make this an independent replication. The re-analysis's point that the hypothesis was generated from these offices is answered only partly. The report should state the outcome window. Months 12–24 alone, after registration, would make the stronger case.
- **More office-months do not mean more independent data.** The effective sample is still 14 offices. With so few clusters, the method used for the mediation confidence intervals matters, and should be reported.
- **Confounding remains.** Office-level management quality could affect both meeting cuts and output. The Limitations section says so, but the Summary still says "confirms".
- **The comparison is overstated.** Meetings (28–66%) and fatigue (2–34%) have overlapping intervals, and their difference is untested. "Less than half as much" describes the point estimates only.

**A simple accounting check is worth reporting.** If meetings produced no case output:
- non-meeting hours in treated offices fell about 3.3%, from about 30.5 to about 29.5 using timesheet levels;
- output fell 3.4%;
- so output per non-meeting hour barely changed.

Read that way, nearly all of the per-hour gain would be removed meeting time, against the mediation model's 47%. The gap implies either that meetings had real productive value or that the model is misspecified. Either way, the authors should address it.

### 5. The counter-arm costing ignores how the per-hour gain arose

The county estimated that restoring service would take 12% more staff.
- **The figure assumes the per-hour gain persists.** With actual hours down 17%, 1.12 × 0.83 = 0.93 of baseline staff-hours. That covers demand only if the counters' per-hour gain of about 7% persists.
- **That gain was largely utilisation.** Busier staff and longer queues produced it. Restoring waiting times means more idle capacity, so most of the gain would disappear. With no per-hour gain, about 20% more staff would be needed (1 / 0.83).
- **The 9% cost figure is unexplained.** 12% more staff at full pay raises cost per contact by 9% only if non-staff costs are about a quarter of the total. That assumption should be stated.

### 6. Halden follow-up

**The "survivors twice over" framing is honest. Three additions would help:**
- **Attrition from the subset.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded, which adds a third layer of selection.
- **A figure that keeps the reverters in.** Including the three reverters at their output at reversion (about 89.5) gives roughly (11 × 96.8 + 3 × 89.5) / 14 ≈ **95.2** for output across all 14.
- **No trend claim.** The rise from 10.8% in the re-analysis to 11.8% here comes from dropping the reverters, not from improvement over time.

**The Summary also overstates who reverted.** It says all three had "client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency cited *client deadlines*. That is deadline-bound work, which the meta-analysis would classify as discretionary. Grouping it under coverage makes the work-type pattern look cleaner than it is.

### 7. Conflict of interest and the attrition correction

R. Okafor co-authored the Halden working paper and now co-authors a report that partly rebuts the critique of it. That is legitimate, but it should be disclosed. The report should also acknowledge that the re-analysis's attrition finding was correct: withdrawals happened after the schedule began, not before. That is an error in the original paper, and the report does not address it.

### 8. Points carried over from the nine-month report

- **Quality is still reported as levels.** Treated and control levels at a single time (3.2% v 3.0%) need a difference-in-differences estimate with a confidence interval.
- **Resignations were not a registered outcome.**
- **Sick days fall mechanically** with fewer scheduled days. They should be reported per scheduled day.
- **The inference method for 14 clusters is still not stated.**

## The rebuttals in Section 5

**Against the re-analysis:** This is convincing. The 24-month estimate meets the standards the re-analysis itself recommended (randomised design, record-based output, strict hours measure, two-year follow-up), and it still finds +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). One nuance: the re-analysis extrapolated *energy* to baseline, not the output gain to zero. The report's wording ("as an extrapolation of self-reported energy had suggested") is fair, but "falling to zero by month ten" should be attributed carefully.

**Against the meta-analysis:** This is also convincing, and it confirms the problem I raised. All four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so they cannot speak to decay. Saying the gain "declined by about a quarter" is accurate as a point estimate. It should carry the caveats from points 1 and 2.

## Where the five documents now leave things

| Question | Current best answer |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work, rigorously measured | About 8–10% at 24 months (Varden logs: 8.5%; meta-analysis, controlled studies: 9.6%) |
| Per-worker output, discretionary work | Slightly below control (−2% to −3.5%), with intervals that include zero |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per worker falls about 9–11% and waits rise; Varden's county ended its counter arm |
| Decay | Some decline, about a quarter from 9 to 24 months, in one trial with a contaminated control group; not to zero |
| Mechanism | Meeting reduction is the leading candidate; fatigue contributes less. Not established, given the confounding and the same-office test |
| Can reorganisation alone deliver the gain? | Untested. The two-office meeting audit hints yes, partly. A trial with a "reorganise without cutting hours" arm is the obvious next study |
| Effect of weak measurement | Scheduled hours plus manager ratings roughly double the apparent per-hour gain |

The Halden headline (+23.4%, "sector-general") is not supported. The re-analysis's "entirely an artifact" is not supported either. A durable gain of roughly 8–10% per hour in discretionary work is the best-supported conclusion. It is probably driven substantially by cutting low-value time, and that kind of change might be achievable without cutting hours.

I can draft a three-arm trial design (reduced hours, meeting reorganisation at full hours, control), or a referee report on this field report.
